hero.title: FEMOS — the agentic operating layer for last-mile women's healthcare
hero.sub: India already has health workers, diagnostic devices, doctors and public-health platforms. Nothing stitches them together. FEMOS does — agents do the mechanical work, people decide faster, and fewer women are lost between screening, review and follow-up.
problem.title: Women are lost in the gaps between visits.
problem.lead: A woman's information and follow-up get lost as she moves between home, community, clinic and district. Readings are copied by hand from device screens. Her history is incomplete. Referrals are not tracked. The same data is typed twice into government systems.
problem.stat1: of women aged 15–49 in India are anaemic
problem.stat2: of adolescent girls aged 15–19 are anaemic
what.title: A layer that connects what already exists.
what.lead: FEMOS is an open-source, offline-first agentic AI layer. It turns readings from existing instruments and multilingual histories into verified health records, prepares clinician-ready cases, and coordinates authorised follow-up through existing systems.
what.quote: Rather than replacing healthcare workers or medical systems, FEMOS makes them work together.
how.title: Six steps from a screen reading to a tracked follow-up.
how.lead: Each step leaves a record, and every step works offline.
found.title: Six foundations, each with one clear job.
found.lead: They are separate parts, so a programme can adopt the pieces it needs and keep the systems it already runs.
kit.title: Integration, not new hardware.
kit.lead: The kit is software, a printed setup card and, only where needed, a validated device bought locally. FEMOS reads the haemoglobin meters, BP monitors and glucometers clinics already use, in whichever way each one allows.
kit.note: A device is called “validated” only after FEMOS has been tested on physical units, with real photos and readings, under a published protocol. Today nothing is validated: adapters are tested on synthetic images and specification byte vectors. Prices are planning estimates to confirm with local suppliers.
arch.title: The engine owns the case. Agents only propose.
arch.lead: A durable workflow engine keeps the case state, the event log and the protocol rules. Agents read from it and propose actions; the engine carries them out only after a person approves.
agents.title: Six agents, each with a narrow job.
agents.lead: They do the mechanical work that takes a health worker's time away from the woman in front of her.
learn.title: One record per woman shows what no single visit can.
learn.lead: A longitudinal record across every touchpoint makes slow signals visible: a falling haemoglobin trend, warning signs that matter only together, missed screenings, referrals that have stalled.
why.title: Not another health OS.
why.lead: General platforms such as OpenSRP, OpenMRS, CommCare and Google's Open Health Stack already exist, and FEMOS connects to them. What is missing is a layer designed around the ways women's care actually fails.
anaemia.title: Anaemia is a doorway, not a single disease.
anaemia.lead: It is common, it can be measured with devices already in the field, and it connects to many other conditions that share the same roots.
results.title: Benchmarks, reported as they are.
results.lead: These numbers come from automated runs on synthetic data. They show whether the software behaves as designed. They are not clinical evidence.
status.title: What is built, and what comes next.
status.lead: FEMOS is an engineering prototype. Everything below runs on synthetic data.
safety.title: What FEMOS will not do.
safety.lead: These limits are part of the design, not settings to be switched off later.
open.title: Open, auditable, and not tied to one model.
open.lead: FEMOS is licensed under Apache-2.0. It uses open-weight models by default and can use others through one adapter. Every dependency and model weight goes through a licence audit.
footer.disclaimer: FEMOS is an engineering prototype using synthetic data. It is not a medical device and must not be used for patient care. FEMOS is independent and is not affiliated with or endorsed by UNICEF, WHO or the Government of India.
